co_red_wall.blurb: A compact bouldering wall on Flagstaff Mountain above Boulder, a couple of minutes' uphill walk from the road. The main face is a steep wall of pockets and small holds, roughly twelve feet tall, with an undercut base and a tree at its right edge, and it is regarded as some of the finest stone on the mountain. All 17 problems are boulders, from the easiest grade up to V10, though most fall between V4 and V9, so this is a place for stronger climbers rather than beginners. Several lines are traverses or tightly defined variations, and some low starts have eroded enough to need a tall reach or extra pads.

co_base_of_2nd_flatiron_boulders.blurb: A string of short boulders alongside the trail at the foot of the Second Flatiron, just west of Boulder, filed under the Satellite Boulders group. The problems are divided among named blocks that run east along the path toward the Wave Boulder. All 17 are bouldering, and the spread is friendly: about half are V0 to V2, with a handful of V3 to V5 problems and a couple of harder ones topping out near V7. It is close to the Chautauqua trailhead, so it works well for a quick session. One walk-in is steeper and busier, while the longer route along the Bluebell Baird trail is easier and quieter.

co_park_view_dome.blurb: The westernmost dome of the Staunton Rocks group inside Staunton State Park. The granite here gives long, moderate, multipitch climbing with wide views, often compared to a Flatiron. The 17 routes split between bolted lines (nine) and traditional lines (eight), and they sit in an easy range: roughly 5.5 to 5.8, with most at 5.7, so it suits newer leaders and parties wanting a mellow day on rock. Reach the dome by following the climber access trail past the Meadow Dome to the far western end, where it is the last dome before the path bends south into the meadow.

co_3_trailhead_wall.blurb: The first section of Monitor Rock that you meet when walking up from Highway 82 on Independence Pass, at roughly 10,000 feet. The granite is good and the approach is nearly nonexistent. Eleven of its 17 routes are bolted and six are traditional, with a few easier lines but most of the grades sitting in the 5.11 range, plus some 5.10 and 5.12. Routes run from about 100 feet to a five-pitch line of around 450 feet. Sun exposure on Monitor Rock is generally excellent, and because it sits lower than the pass the season runs a little longer.
co_3_trailhead_wall.parking_note: Park beside Highway 82 on the west side of Monitor Rock, a few hundred feet beyond Mount Elbert Lodge as you drive west; a well-worn trail leads up to the wall.

co_river_wall_2.blurb: A short wall in Elevenmile Canyon, about six miles up the canyon road beside the river. It holds a varied mix of bolted and traditional lines, plus one boulder problem at the base, and the grades are wide: easy 5.5 climbs through to several 5.12s, with the bulk in the 5.8 to 5.11 range. Routes are short, you can lower from the anchors or walk off, and top-rope setups are possible from above. At around 8,500 feet the canyon runs cooler than most Front Range crags. High water can make the river-side route in awkward.

co_dynamite_cliff_band.blurb: Sandstone problems along a band of cliff in the Dynamite Shacks bouldering, close to Colorado National Monument's eastern entrance outside Grand Junction. It has 16 boulder problems and a single roped line. The bouldering ranges from V1 to V7, with most problems in the V2 to V4 range and a few harder ones near the top end, so there is something for a mixed group. The Dynamite Shacks area is dry and climbable through much of the year, though the hillsides turn very muddy after rain or snowmelt.
